documents.title: The paradox of the paperless office
documents.text:
Thirty years ago, forecasters promised that computers would banish paper from the workplace. Today, most offices consume more of it than ever, and a recent survey of two thousand firms suggests that the habit is not merely stubborn but, in some respects, rational.

Researchers who observed staff at work found that people print documents not out of ignorance but when a task demands careful attention: reviewing a contract, comparing two budgets, or marking a draft. On a screen, they noted, readers tend to skim, and errors that would be caught on paper often slip through. One accountant described printing a spreadsheet as "the only way I can see what is wrong with it".

The cost, however, is considerable. Paper, toner and storage account for a surprising share of overheads, and the files kept in cabinets are frequently duplicated in digital form, so that no one knows which version is authoritative. Several firms have therefore adopted a compromise: a printing budget for each department, with no restriction on how it is spent. Early results show a reduction of a third in paper use, with no rise in complaints.

The lesson, according to the study's authors, is that policies forbidding paper tend to fail, because they treat a working method as a bad habit. Policies that make it a considered choice appear to succeed.

questions.prompt: What is the central point of the article?
choices: Offices should ban printing in all departments
Computers have failed to improve office work
Paper endures because it suits some careful tasks
Staff print documents out of plain ignorance
questions.explanation: The article shows paper use is tied to careful tasks, and suggests managing it rather than banning it.

questions.prompt: Why do the accountants print spreadsheets?
choices: Mistakes are easier to notice on paper
The software cannot open large files
Managers insist on printed copies
The printing is free for staff
questions.explanation: On screen readers skim and errors slip through; printing shows what is wrong.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the departmental budgets?
choices: They forced staff to stop printing entirely
They doubled the cost of paper in each unit
They were rejected by most employees
They cut waste without banning printing
questions.explanation: Paper use fell by a third with no rise in complaints and no restriction on spending.

questions.prompt: What do the authors think about bans on paper?
choices: They always succeed when applied in large firms
They often fail by ignoring working methods
They are popular with most employees
They reduce overheads far more than budgets
questions.explanation: Bans treat a working method as a bad habit.

documents.title: Application for a transfer to the Lyon office
documents.text:
Dear Ms. Delacroix-Hart,

I am writing to apply for the vacancy for Senior Financial Analyst at the Lyon office, which was announced internally on 6 May. I have worked in the Manchester team for six years, the last three as a senior member, and I believe my experience would suit the role.

Over the past eighteen months, I led the project that merged our reporting procedures with those of the Lisbon subsidiary, a task that involved reconciling two accounting systems and training twenty colleagues. The project finished a month ahead of schedule, and it reduced the time needed to close the quarterly accounts by almost two days. I should add that I am fluent in French, having studied at a university in Grenoble, and that I have visited the Lyon office several times for joint meetings.

I recognize that the post is advertised as requiring seven years' experience, one more than I have. I would suggest, however, that the breadth of my work on the Lisbon project compensates for the difference, and I would be glad to discuss this with you. My manager, Mr. Hargreaves, is aware of my application and has indicated that he would support it, though he would need two months to find a replacement.

I enclose my CV and look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Ewa Kowalczyk

choices: To resign from the company next month
To apply for a post at another office
To complain about the conduct of a manager
To ask for a salary increase this year
questions.explanation: She applies for the Senior Financial Analyst vacancy in Lyon.

questions.explanation: It reduced the time to close the quarterly accounts by almost two days.

questions.explanation: She is fluent in French and has visited the Lyon office; it supports her suitability.

questions.explanation: The post requires seven years and she has six, but she says her breadth compensates.

documents.title: Policy on data retention for customers of Stratus Cloud
documents.text:
How long do we keep your data? The answer depends on what kind of data it is and on whether you have closed your account.

Files and content that you upload are stored for as long as your account remains active. If you close your account, your files are deleted from our live servers within thirty days. Copies held in backup systems are overwritten on a rolling basis and will have disappeared entirely within a further ninety days. During this period, the backups are not accessible to our staff except where required by law.

Billing records, including invoices and payment dates, are kept for seven years after the transaction, because tax regulations oblige us to do so. They do not contain the content of your files. Technical logs, which record when and from where you logged in, are kept for twelve months to help us investigate security incidents; after that, they are anonymized so that they can no longer be linked to you.

You may ask us at any time to export or delete your data. Requests are normally completed within five working days, though we may ask you to confirm your identity first. We are unable to delete data that we are legally required to keep, but we will tell you which data this applies to and for how long.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the page?
choices: To announce a security breach to users
To advertise a cheaper storage plan online
To describe how to upload files safely
To explain how long data is kept
questions.explanation: The page lists retention periods for files, billing records and logs.

questions.prompt: How long after account closure do backups disappear completely?
choices: Within thirty days of the closure date

questions.explanation: Files are removed within thirty days and backups within a further ninety days.

choices: They contain the files that users upload

questions.explanation: Tax regulations oblige the company to keep them for seven years.

They are kept for seven years
questions.explanation: After twelve months they are anonymized so they cannot be linked to you.

documents.title: Chat between an editor and an author
documents.text:
Marianne Voss [11:02]: Good morning, Daniel. I've finished the first read of chapter nine, and I think it's the best chapter in the book. The argument finally has a shape.

Daniel Achterberg [11:05]: That's a relief. I rewrote it three times. Did the section on the 1920s crisis work?

Marianne Voss [11:07]: Largely, yes. My only worry is the paragraph on page 212 where you say that the bank "could not have foreseen" the collapse. Elsewhere in the chapter you show that two directors warned of it in writing.

Daniel Achterberg [11:10]: Good catch. I meant that the board could not have foreseen it, not the directors individually. I'll make the distinction clear.

Marianne Voss [11:12]: Please do, because a reviewer will certainly notice. And, while you're there, could you cut the footnote about the lawsuit? It's interesting but it interrupts the argument.

Daniel Achterberg [11:14]: I'd prefer to keep it, perhaps moved to the notes at the back.

Marianne Voss [11:15]: That works. When can I expect the revised chapter?

Daniel Achterberg [11:17]: Friday morning, if nothing else comes up.

questions.prompt: What is the editor's main reaction to the chapter?
choices: She finds it strong but queries one point
She wants it rewritten from the beginning
She thinks it should be left out of the book
She finds the argument still unclear
questions.explanation: She praises it and flags one contradiction and a footnote.

questions.prompt: What is the inconsistency on page 212?
choices: The date of the crisis is given wrongly twice
The lawsuit is described in two chapters
The bank 'could not foresee' what was warned
Two directors are said to have resigned
questions.explanation: The text says the bank could not have foreseen collapse but shows two directors warned of it.

questions.prompt: What does the author's reply imply?
choices: He disagrees with the editor's reading of it
He meant the board, not each director
He intends to remove the paragraph entirely
He has not read his own chapter closely
questions.explanation: He meant 'the board could not have foreseen it, not the directors individually'.

questions.prompt: What is agreed about the footnote?
choices: It will be deleted before the proof stage

It will be written again by the editor
It will be moved to the back notes
questions.explanation: The author prefers keeping it in the notes at the back, and the editor says that works.

documents.title: The stubborn appeal of the commuter railway
documents.text:
When engineers proposed the Ellsworth line in the 1990s, critics called it a relic: a rail route to a city whose centre was losing jobs to the suburbs. Two decades later, the line carries more passengers than any other in the region, and the authorities are planning a second track.

The reasons are only partly the ones that planners foresaw. The line was expected to serve commuters, and it does, but it has also become a route for students, who travel to three colleges along its length, and for retired residents making daytime trips for appointments and shopping. Because trains run every fifteen minutes, many passengers no longer consult a timetable, a habit that transport specialists say is the best indicator of a successful service.

Not all the results have been welcome. House prices near the stations have risen by almost half, pushing out some of the residents the line was meant to help. A study found that nearly a third of those living within walking distance of the stops are now new arrivals, mostly younger professionals.

The authorities say that they will require developers of new housing near the stations to include affordable homes, though similar rules elsewhere have been difficult to enforce.

choices: A line was cancelled after local protests

questions.explanation: The article details unexpected success and rising house prices.

choices: Frequent trains mean riders need not plan ahead

questions.explanation: With trains every fifteen minutes, many no longer consult a timetable, an indicator of success.

questions.explanation: Similar rules elsewhere have been difficult to enforce.

documents.title: Proposal to introduce core hours
documents.text:
MEMORANDUM
To: Department Heads
From: Sunita Raghavan, Human Resources Director
Subject: Proposal to introduce core hours

I am writing to propose that the company replace its present arrangement of fully flexible working hours with a system of core hours, under which all staff would be expected to be available between 10 a.m. and 3 p.m., while remaining free to arrange the remainder of their day.

The proposal responds to complaints that I have received from several departments. Under the present system, staff may begin work at any time between 7 a.m. and 11 a.m., and it is not unusual for a meeting to be impossible to arrange because no two members of a team are present at once. A survey of fifty managers found that nearly two thirds had abandoned at least one meeting in the past month for this reason.

I should stress that the proposal is not intended to abolish flexibility. Employees who need to adjust their hours for family or medical reasons would be able to apply for an exemption, and no one would be required to work longer than at present. I recognize that some staff, particularly those who commute from far away, may find the change inconvenient.

I would be grateful for your comments by the end of the month, after which I shall prepare a proposal for the executive committee.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the memo?
choices: To cancel flexible hours for every employee
To propose a shared period of availability
To increase the length of the working week
To announce a new bus for commuters
questions.explanation: Core hours of 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. would apply to all staff.

questions.prompt: Why is the change proposed?
choices: Staff have asked for longer working hours
Managers want to monitor attendance closely
The offices will close earlier in the day
Teams struggle to find times for meetings
questions.explanation: Meetings become impossible when no two team members are present at once.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about employees with family needs?
choices: They could seek an exemption from core hours

They would lose all of their flexibility

questions.explanation: Employees needing to adjust hours for family or medical reasons may apply for an exemption.

questions.prompt: What does Ms. Raghavan acknowledge?
choices: The survey of managers was not reliable

Long commutes may make the change harder
Managers will resist the change strongly
questions.explanation: She notes that those commuting from far away may find the change inconvenient.

documents.title: A reissue that deserves its second life
documents.text:
When The Salt Roads first appeared in 1974, it sold modestly and was forgotten within a decade. Its reissue this month, with a foreword by one of the novelists it influenced, is a welcome act of rescue. The book follows a family of salt traders across a mountain pass over a single year, and it is remarkable for its refusal to dramatize what it describes.

Where a modern novelist might turn a blizzard into a set piece, Hanna Ruiz gives it a paragraph, and the reader is made to feel the weight of days through repetition: the loading of the mules, the counting of coins, the evening arguments about prices. The effect is hypnotic, though it may test the patience of those who expect a plot. The second half, in which a daughter quietly defies her father's choice of husband, is the most moving, precisely because the author withholds any comment.

The foreword is less successful. It spends too much time on the writer's own debt to the book and too little on the book itself. The edition also lacks a map, a serious omission in a novel so concerned with geography.

These are small objections. The Salt Roads is a work of unusual calm, and it is good that it is once more available to readers.

questions.prompt: What is the reviewer's overall judgment?
choices: The book was a bestseller when it appeared
The novel is too dull to be recommended
The reissue is better than the original
The novel is calm and worth reissuing
questions.explanation: The reviewer calls the reissue 'a welcome act of rescue' and praises the book.

choices: She gives it the whole of the second half
She gives it a paragraph, without drama
She uses it to bring the novel to a close
She leaves it out of the story entirely
questions.explanation: Ruiz gives it a paragraph.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about readers who like plots?
choices: They will love the second half

They will prefer the map
questions.explanation: The effect is hypnotic 'though it may test the patience of those who expect a plot'.

questions.explanation: The edition lacks a map, a serious omission in a novel so concerned with geography.

documents.title: Orchard Row Care Home: a different way to grow older
documents.text:
Choosing a care home is among the hardest decisions a family can make, and we do not pretend that it is easy. At Orchard Row, we have tried to build a place where residents feel that they have moved house, not entered an institution.

Rooms are single, with private bathrooms, and residents are encouraged to bring their own furniture. Meals are cooked on site from ingredients grown in our gardens, and anyone who wishes may help in the kitchen or the vegetable beds. There are no fixed visiting hours: relatives are welcome whenever they come, and may share a meal with the resident for a modest charge.

Our staff-to-resident ratio is higher than the national average, and every resident has a named member of staff who knows their routines and preferences. We are not a nursing home, however, and we cannot care for those who need continuous medical attention. In such cases, we will help the family to find a suitable place and, where possible, remain in contact.

We invite you to visit without appointment on any weekday and to stay for lunch. We would rather you saw us as we are, on an ordinary day.

documents.title: The case against the open-plan hospital ward
documents.text:
For decades, the large open ward, with beds ranged along both walls under the eye of a single nurse, was the standard of hospital design. It was cheap to build and made supervision easy. Today, a growing body of research suggests that it was neither as efficient nor as safe as its defenders believed.

Studies comparing wards of the traditional kind with those composed of single rooms have found that infections spread more readily in the former, and that patients in open wards sleep less, with measurable effects on recovery. Patients also report that the lack of privacy makes them reluctant to discuss symptoms, a barrier that may delay diagnosis.

Defenders of the old design make a fair point: in a single room, a deteriorating patient can go unnoticed, and nurses walk considerably farther in a day. Several new hospitals have addressed this by installing sensors and by arranging rooms around a central station with glass walls, so that staff retain a view of every door.

The cost remains the obstacle. Single-room wards require roughly a third more floor space, and health authorities with ageing buildings must decide whether to replace them or to adapt what they have.

questions.prompt: What is the article mainly about?
choices: The history of nursing in public hospitals

The cost of training nurses for wards
questions.explanation: The article reviews research against open wards and the drawbacks of single rooms.

questions.prompt: What did studies find about infections?

questions.explanation: Infections spread more readily in the traditional wards.

choices: Patients sleep less well than in open wards

A patient's decline may pass unnoticed there
questions.explanation: In a single room a deteriorating patient can go unnoticed, and nurses walk farther.

questions.prompt: What is the main obstacle to change?
choices: Nurses refuse to work in the new wards
Single rooms need more space and funding
Patients still prefer open wards to single rooms
Sensors are too unreliable to depend on
questions.explanation: They require roughly a third more floor space, and the cost remains the obstacle.
